When it's so easy to make beer, though, why pay four times what you would to make your own? A bucket and a stock pot is all I'd use for 5gal batches. It's basically brew-in-a-bag, but if you have a supply near-by you can get your grain bill for a 5gal batch for about $40. Generally, Local Homebrew Store(hereafter LHS) will grind your grain for you. At Lowes hardware(or any bigbox hardware store) they sell 5gal nylon paint strainer bags, 2 for ~$3. You'll need maybe four for a 5gal batch and a couple 1gal bags for your hops. While you're there, pick up one of their 5gal plastic bucket with lid or if you have a restaurant friend, almost any food-grade bucket will work. The bucket will be your fermenter. You'll need a yardsale or craigslist turkey cooker, usually around $20 or so but it has to have a 5gal pot with it. If you can, find a stainless steel turkey fryer and you can skip the bucket. My dad and I had a 25gal stainless pot that we mashed and fermented in. You could definitely do less than 5gal, I've used a three gallon pot for lower alcohol 5gal batches, but big beers will need space for the grain to absorb the water. You'll also need a long spoon, a thermometer that goes to at least 180F, a recipe, and about 5 hours to commit.

A quick note about sanitation: The secret to good beer isn't hop additions or exotic fruit adjuncts or overalls or beards, it's sanitation. Always wash your hands. Always clean your pot, bucket, spoon, thermometer, and anything else you might touch your beer with and sanitize, sanitize, sanitize. A simple disinfectant can be made in your fermenting bucket with four gallons of cold water and a half capful of chlorine bleach. This is just to sanitize your tools and pot, not to make beer out of, so dispose of it before adding your beer to your fermenter.

So, now that you have your recipe and your ground grains and hops, you'll split your grains up between the sanitized paint bags and add them to 90F water in your pot. You'll be bringing the heat up slowly for the next 90-120 minutes, with each level taking 30mins each with the possibility of extending the last step. More on that in a bit. The first temp level is 90F-115F. This is the acid rest, important for adjusting the ph of the water. The second level is the protein rest which creates the enzymes that will be eating the starch and converting it to sugar and it goes from 115F-135F. The final stage is the sugar rest and it runs from 135F-170F. The sugar rest has a wide range of temperature but the thing to know is 135-148 creates a high alcohol/light body wort while 148-158 makes for a low alcohol/ heavy body wort. The lower temps allow the enzymes to convert more starch to sugar so the longer you stay low the more sugary your wort. You can also hold it at those temps if you're not sure that all the starch has converted to sugar. You'll want to stir every once in awhile, but you're using low heat to bring it up gradually so your bags shouldn't melt unless they sit on a hot spot too long. When you're satisfied(I always tasted it. Sweet=beer) remove the grain bags and squeeze or drip them back into the pot. You can also put a gallon of fresh water in your fermenter and rinse your grain in it, then add it back to get all the sugar you can.

So, you've squoze your bags and there's about 5gal of sweet brown water in your pot. Now, bring it to a boil and add your hops (put them in your 1gal strainer bags to make clean up and transfer cleaner and easier) according to the directions in your recipe(your recipe will have most of this other than my time and temp schedule). When your boil time is over, remove your hop sacks and either transfer to your bucket or put the lid on and let it cool to 70F. When it's 70F(some of our bigger batches took two days to cool but if you leave the lid on, nothing gets in) pitch the yeast by sprinkling it on top of the wort and put the lid back on. If your using the bucket, don't press the lid on tight. Set it on top where gas can escape but nothing gets in. Let it ferment for two-three weeks for ales(which I highly recommend as a first beer, super easy) and then start drinking. You can bottle it, keg it, or drink it out of the bucket. I save 2L soda bottles and fill them with a siphon hose. As long as they're clean, you should have some great beer. Let them sit in the bottles for a week, then refrigerate as needed.
